claim: Langerhans cells are specialized antigen-presenting cells localized within the epidermis and mucosal epithelium.
source: Langerhans cells are specialized antigen-presenting cells localized within the epidermis and mucosal epithelium.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Langerhans cells.

claim: Upon contact with Langerhans cells, pathogens are captured by the C-type lectin langerin.
source: Upon contact with Langerhans cells, pathogens are captured by the C-type lectin langerin and internalized into a structurally unique vesicle known as a Birbeck granule.
evidence: This is established knowledge about langerin function.

claim: Pathogens captured by langerin are internalized into a structurally unique vesicle known as a Birbeck granule.
source: Upon contact with Langerhans cells, pathogens are captured by the C-type lectin langerin and internalized into a structurally unique vesicle known as a Birbeck granule.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Birbeck granules.

claim: The mechanism by which the characteristic zippered membrane structure of Birbeck granules is formed remains elusive.
source: Although the immunological role of Langerhans cells and Birbeck granules have been extensively studied, the mechanism by which the characteristic zippered membrane structure of Birbeck granules is formed remains elusive.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The 3D structure of the repeating unit of the honeycomb lattice of langerin was reconstructed at 6.4 Å resolution using cryo-electron tomography.
source: In this study, we observed isolated Birbeck granules using cryo-electron tomography and reconstructed the 3D structure of the repeating unit of the honeycomb lattice of langerin at 6.4 Å resolution.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The interaction between two langerin trimers is mediated by docking the flexible loop at residues 258–263 into the secondary carbohydrate-binding cleft.
source: We found that the interaction between the two langerin trimers was mediated by docking the flexible loop at residues 258–263 into the secondary carbohydrate-binding cleft.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on structural data from cryo-electron tomography.

claim: Mutations within the loop at residues 258-263 inhibited Birbeck granule formation.
source: Mutations within the loop inhibited Birbeck granule formation and the internalization of HIV pseudovirus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claim: Mutations within the loop at residues 258-263 inhibited the internalization of HIV pseudovirus.
source: Mutations within the loop inhibited Birbeck granule formation and the internalization of HIV pseudovirus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from virus internalization assays.

claim: Langerhans cells capture pathogens by recognizing their surface mannose-containing oligosaccharides via langerin.
source: In these tissues, specialized antigen-presenting cells called Langerhans cells capture pathogens by recognizing their surface mannose-containing oligosaccharides via the C-type lectin langerin (Valladeau et al., 2003; Doebel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Birbeck granules have a central striated lamella between closely apposed membranes.
source: Pathogens internalized via langerin are enclosed in a specialized organelle called a Birbeck granule, which has a central striated lamella between closely apposed membranes (Birbeck et al., 1961; Valladeau et al., 2000; McDermott et al., 2004; Valladeau et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Once pathogens are captured, Langerhans cells undergo maturation and migrate to peripheral lymph nodes.
source: Once pathogens are captured, Langerhans cells undergo maturation and migrate to peripheral lymph nodes, where they present processed antigens to T cells (Merad et al., 2008; de Jong et al., 2010; Rhodes et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Langerhans cells present processed antigens to T cells in peripheral lymph nodes.
source: Once pathogens are captured, Langerhans cells undergo maturation and migrate to peripheral lymph nodes, where they present processed antigens to T cells (Merad et al., 2008; de Jong et al., 2010; Rhodes et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Langerin is a type II transmembrane protein composed of a cytoplasmic tail, coiled-coil neck region, and carbohydrate recognition domain (CRD).
source: Langerin is a type II transmembrane protein that is composed of a cytoplasmic tail, coiled-coil neck region, and carbohydrate recognition domain (CRD) (Stambach and Taylor, 2003; Valladeau et al., 1999; Valladeau et al., 2000; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Langerin forms a trimer through the coiled-coil neck region.
source: Through the coiled-coil neck region, langerin forms a trimer, which is functionally important for oligosaccharide binding (Stambach and Taylor, 2003; Weis and Drickamer, 1996; Weis and Drickamer, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Langerin trimer formation is functionally important for oligosaccharide binding.
source: Through the coiled-coil neck region, langerin forms a trimer, which is functionally important for oligosaccharide binding (Stambach and Taylor, 2003; Weis and Drickamer, 1996; Weis and Drickamer, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The calcium-dependent carbohydrate-binding capacity of langerin CRD is essential for the formation of Birbeck granules.
source: The calcium-dependent carbohydrate-binding capacity of langerin CRD is essential for the formation of Birbeck granules because the removal of calcium ions causes them to unzip and disintegrate (Stambach and Taylor, 2003; Bartosik, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Removal of calcium ions causes Birbeck granules to unzip and disintegrate.
source: The calcium-dependent carbohydrate-binding capacity of langerin CRD is essential for the formation of Birbeck granules because the removal of calcium ions causes them to unzip and disintegrate (Stambach and Taylor, 2003; Bartosik, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The 'face-to-face' interaction between langerin trimers via CRDs confers the characteristic zippered membranes with a central striation of Birbeck granules.
source: It has been proposed that the 'face-to-face' interaction between the langerin trimers via CRDs confers the characteristic zippered membranes with a central striation of Birbeck granules (Thépaut et al., 2009' Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a previously proposed model cited from literature and illustrated in figures.

claim: Langerin's high affinity for mannose and oligo-mannose allows Langerhans cells to capture a wide range of pathogens.
source: Langerin's high affinity for mannose and oligo-mannose allows Langerhans cells to capture a wide range of pathogens, including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Candida albicans, Mycobacterium leprae, herpes simplex virus, and human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) (Tateno et al., 2010; Hunger et al., 2004; de Jong and Geijtenbeek, 2010; de Witte et al., 2007; Turville et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Langerin can capture Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Candida albicans, Mycobacterium leprae, herpes simplex virus, and HIV-1.
source: Langerin's high affinity for mannose and oligo-mannose allows Langerhans cells to capture a wide range of pathogens, including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Candida albicans, Mycobacterium leprae, herpes simplex virus, and human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) (Tateno et al., 2010; Hunger et al., 2004; de Jong and Geijtenbeek, 2010; de Witte et al., 2007; Turville et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Langerhans cells in the mucosa are the initial target of HIV-1 in sexually transmitted infections.
source: Although Langerhans cells in the mucosa are the initial target of HIV-1 in sexually transmitted infections, the efficiency of Langerhans cell infection is low, requiring high viral loads of HIV-1 to infect cells (Kawamura et al., 2001; Kawamura et al., 2000; Ogawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The efficiency of Langerhans cell infection by HIV-1 is low, requiring high viral loads.
source: Although Langerhans cells in the mucosa are the initial target of HIV-1 in sexually transmitted infections, the efficiency of Langerhans cell infection is low, requiring high viral loads of HIV-1 to infect cells (Kawamura et al., 2001; Kawamura et al., 2000; Ogawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The resistance of Langerhans cells to HIV-1 infection is mediated by the efficient internalization of HIV-1 into Birbeck granules and subsequent autophagic degradation.
source: The resistance of Langerhans cells to HIV-1 infection is mediated by the efficient internalization of HIV-1 into Birbeck granules and subsequent autophagic degradation (de Witte et al., 2007; Ribeiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Exogenous expression of langerin in mammalian cell lines readily reproduces the formation of Birbeck granules.
source: Exogenous expression of langerin in mammalian cell lines readily reproduces the formation of Birbeck granules (McDermott et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Addition of yeast mannan to langerin-expressing cells enhances the formation of large Birbeck granules.
source: We found that the addition of yeast mannan to langerin-expressing cells enhances the formation of large Birbeck granules (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Isolated Birbeck granules are thin lamellar vesicles of assorted sizes under cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Under cryo-electron microscopy, the isolated Birbeck granules were observed to be thin lamellar vesicles of assorted sizes, similar to those reported previously (Figure 1E and F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Sagebiel and Reed, 1968; Lenormand et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study supported by imaging data and citations.

claim: Birbeck granules appear wavy, suggesting structural heterogeneity.
source: Unlike regular 2D crystals of proteins, Birbeck granules appear wavy, suggesting structural heterogeneity.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed structural features.

claim: 2D classification of Birbeck granules showed nearly three-fold symmetrical arrangements of pores with a diameter of approximately 10 nm.
source: The 2D classification of the segmented images extracted from the micrographs showed nearly three-fold symmetrical arrangements of pores with a diameter of approximately 10 nm; however, no clear crystalline lattice was observed (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from image analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: No clear crystalline lattice was observed in 2D classification of Birbeck granules.
source: The 2D classification of the segmented images extracted from the micrographs showed nearly three-fold symmetrical arrangements of pores with a diameter of approximately 10 nm; however, no clear crystalline lattice was observed (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from image analysis.

claim: Some Birbeck granules were twisted, providing different views sufficient for 3D reconstruction.
source: Although most Birbeck granules were oriented in approximately the same direction with respect to the beam axis, some granules were twisted, providing different views that were sufficient for 3D reconstruction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data.

claim: The initial density map shows a langerin trimer with three inverted trimers attached to the CRDs.
source: The initial density map (Figure 2A) shows a langerin trimer (blue) with three inverted trimers (red) attached to the CRDs.
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The initial resolution of the density map was limited to approximately 24 Å due to flexibility between each langerin trimer.
source: However, because of the flexibility between each langerin trimer, the resolution was limited to ~24 Å.
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis with an explanation based on structural properties.

claim: Focused refinement and 3D classification improved the resolution to 6.4 Å.
source: To improve the resolution, we generated a mask enclosing the central langerin trimer and three attached CRDs and performed focused refinement and 3D classification (Figure 2B). The resolution was improved to 6.4 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which clearly visualized the alpha helices and enabled us to generate a model based on the previously reported crystal structure of the langerin trimer (Feinberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis.

claim: The 6.4 Å resolution clearly visualized the alpha helices of langerin.
source: The resolution was improved to 6.4 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which clearly visualized the alpha helices and enabled us to generate a model based on the previously reported crystal structure of the langerin trimer (Feinberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis.

claim: A honeycomb lattice model was built based on two-body refinement.
source: We then performed a two-body refinement to visualize the spatial relationship between the two opposing langerin trimers (Nakane et al., 2018). Based on this refinement (Figure 2C), we built a honeycomb lattice model (Figure 2D and Figure 2—video 1), which agrees with the striation of the Birbeck granules observed by ultra-thin section electron microscopy and the ~10 nm pores visualized in the 2D classification images (Figure 1C and G; Birbeck et al., 1961).
evidence: This is a model built from structural data.

claim: The honeycomb lattice model agrees with the striation of Birbeck granules observed by ultra-thin section electron microscopy.
source: Based on this refinement (Figure 2C), we built a honeycomb lattice model (Figure 2D and Figure 2—video 1), which agrees with the striation of the Birbeck granules observed by ultra-thin section electron microscopy and the ~10 nm pores visualized in the 2D classification images (Figure 1C and G; Birbeck et al., 1961).
evidence: This is a comparison between the model and previous observations.

claim: The honeycomb lattice is non-uniform because of structural heterogeneity.
source: However, in reality, the honeycomb lattice is non-uniform because of the structural heterogeneity.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed structural variation.

claim: Loop 258-263 is highly flexible in the crystal structure of langerin.
source: An in-depth analysis of the interaction region between the two CRDs (Figure 3) revealed that the interaction is mediated by a loop at residues 258–263, which is highly flexible in the crystal structure (Feinberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the current structure and citation to previous crystal structure.

claim: The interaction between two CRDs is maintained by docking the loops of two langerin molecules into each other's lateral cleft.
source: The interaction between the two CRDs appears to be maintained by docking the loops of two langerin molecules into each other's lateral cleft, which constitutes the secondary carbohydrate-binding site (Figure 3A, pink circles; Chatwell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis with citation to previous work on the secondary binding site.

claim: The interaction between the two CRDs is flexible, with approximately 30° tilting motion with the loop as the fulcrum.
source: The interaction between the two CRDs is flexible because the first eigenvector of the multi-body analysis represents an approximately 30° tilting motion with the loop as the fulcrum (Figure 3B, and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from multi-body analysis of structural data.

claim: Loop 258-263 of the inverted molecule participates in the secondary carbohydrate-binding site of the upright molecule.
source: Interestingly, loop 258–263 of the inverted molecule appears to participate in the secondary carbohydrate-binding site of the upright molecule (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis.

claim: The secondary calcium-independent binding site has a lower affinity for carbohydrate ligands than the primary calcium-dependent binding site.
source: A previous study found that the secondary calcium-independent binding site has a lower affinity for carbohydrate ligands than the primary calcium-dependent binding site (Chatwell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The docked loop 258-263 may provide additional interactions with the hydroxyl group of mannose via Glu261 and Asp263.
source: The docked loop 258–263 may provide additional interactions with the hydroxyl group of mannose via Glu261 and Asp263, thus increasing the affinity of the secondary binding site when two langerin trimers form a complex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: The docked loop 258-263 may increase the affinity of the secondary binding site when two langerin trimers form a complex.
source: The docked loop 258–263 may provide additional interactions with the hydroxyl group of mannose via Glu261 and Asp263, thus increasing the affinity of the secondary binding site when two langerin trimers form a complex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: The Trp264Arg mutation is associated with a lack of Birbeck granules.
source: Furthermore, the Trp264Arg mutation is associated with a lack of Birbeck granules (Verdijk et al., 2005; Figdor et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Trp264 may be involved in docking the loop into the cleft.
source: Trp264 may also be involved in docking the loop into the cleft; however, it is more likely that disruption of the hydrophobic core of the CRD is responsible for this defect in Birbeck granule formation (Chatwell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation.

claim: Disruption of the hydrophobic core of the CRD is more likely responsible for the defect in Birbeck granule formation caused by Trp264Arg mutation.
source: Trp264 may also be involved in docking the loop into the cleft; however, it is more likely that disruption of the hydrophobic core of the CRD is responsible for this defect in Birbeck granule formation (Chatwell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations with citation.

claim: Three langerin mutants were generated: MRGD (Met260Ala), MRGK (Met260Ala, Glu261Arg), and ARGK (Met260Ala, Glu261Arg, Asp263Lys).
source: To investigate the importance of loop 258–263 in the biogenesis of Birbeck granules, we mutated three residues in the loop: Met260Ala, Glu261Arg, and Asp263Lys, and generated three mutated langerin constructs, each carrying one (MRGD), two (MRGK), or three mutations (ARGK).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: As the number of mutations in loop 258-263 increased, the length of Birbeck granules decreased.
source: As the number of mutations increased, the length of Birbeck granules decreased.
evidence: This is a finding from mutational analysis.

claim: With two point mutations (MRGK), some cross-sections of Birbeck granules became spherical rather than rod-shaped.
source: With two point mutations (MRGK), some cross-sections became spherical rather than rod-shaped, suggesting that the Birbeck granules failed to extend.
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy.

claim: With three mutations (ARGK), clusters of Birbeck granules were not observed, with isolated individual granules observed instead.
source: With three mutations (ARGK), clusters of Birbeck granules were not observed, with isolated individual granules observed instead.
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy.

claim: The number of Birbeck granules showed less significant differences among mutants because numerous short fragments were present in the mutant specimens.
source: In contrast, the number of the Birbeck granules showed less significant differences because numerous short fragments were present in the mutant specimen (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from quantitative analysis with explanation.

claim: HIV pseudoviruses attached to both wild-type and ARGK mutant langerin.
source: The HIV pseudoviruses attached to both wild-type and ARGK mutant langerin and the attachment was abolished by the addition of mannan (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from virus attachment assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Attachment of HIV pseudoviruses to langerin was abolished by the addition of mannan.
source: The HIV pseudoviruses attached to both wild-type and ARGK mutant langerin and the attachment was abolished by the addition of mannan (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from virus attachment assays.

claim: The mutation of loop 258-263 did not disrupt the binding of glycosylated envelope proteins to the primary carbohydrate-binding sites.
source: This indicated that the mutation of the loop did not disrupt the binding of the glycosylated envelope proteins to the primary carbohydrate-binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference from the virus attachment data.

claim: The internalization of HIV pseudovirus was significantly inhibited by the ARGK mutation.
source: In contrast, the internalization of the pseudovirus was significantly inhibited by the ARGK mutation (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from virus internalization assays shown in Figures 5B and C.

claim: Disruption of Birbeck granule formation by the mutation of loop 258-263 inhibited the internalization of HIV pseudovirus.
source: These results suggest that disruption of Birbeck granule formation by the mutation of loop 258–263 inhibited the internalization of HIV pseudovirus.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: N-linked high-mannose oligosaccharides bind to langerin at both primary and secondary carbohydrate-binding sites.
source: A previous study proposed that N-linked high-mannose oligosaccharides bind to langerin at both primary and secondary carbohydrate-binding sites (Chatwell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The proposed model requires bending of the coiled-coil necks of the two langerin trimers to form a complex with HIV-1 env via the high-mannose oligosaccharide.
source: Our model requires bending of the coiled-coil necks of the two langerin trimers to form a complex with HIV-1 env via the high-mannose oligosaccharide (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on structural analysis.

claim: The coiled-coil prediction profile suggests that the N-terminal part of the neck does not necessarily form a rigid triple coiled coil.
source: Although the triple coiled-coil structure of the neck domain does not seem to bend strongly, the coiled-coil prediction profile suggests that the N-terminal part of the neck does not necessarily form a rigid triple coiled coil (Lupas et al., 1991; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction with citation.

claim: The neck region of the langerin trimer is flexible and swings on the cell surface.
source: Thus, we speculate that the neck region of the langerin trimer is flexible and swings on the cell surface, allowing loop 258–263 of one trimer to dock into the cleft of an adjacent trimer.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural features.

claim: Once the triad structure (two langerin trimers and one env protein) is formed, the elasticity of the neck region can deform the cell membrane and initiate invagination.
source: Once the triad structure, consisting of two langerin trimers and one env protein, is formed, the elasticity of the neck region can deform the cell membrane and initiate invagination.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on structural considerations.

claim: The formation of clathrin pits may be involved in membrane invagination during Birbeck granule formation.
source: The formation of clathrin pits may also be involved in membrane invagination, because the cytoplasmic ends of Birbeck granules are coated with clathrin (Mc Dermott et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation.

claim: The cytoplasmic ends of Birbeck granules are coated with clathrin.
source: The formation of clathrin pits may also be involved in membrane invagination, because the cytoplasmic ends of Birbeck granules are coated with clathrin (Mc Dermott et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Other intracellular mechanisms such as the actin cytoskeleton may be involved in membrane deformation during Birbeck granule formation.
source: Additionally, it is possible that other intracellular mechanisms such as the actin cytoskeleton, are involved in this membrane deformation process because annexin A2 is required for the proper formation of Birbeck granules (Thornton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation.

claim: Annexin A2 is required for the proper formation of Birbeck granules.
source: Additionally, it is possible that other intracellular mechanisms such as the actin cytoskeleton, are involved in this membrane deformation process because annexin A2 is required for the proper formation of Birbeck granules (Thornton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The docking of loop 258-263 into the secondary calcium-independent carbohydrate-binding cleft mediates the assembly of the langerin lattice.
source: It is noteworthy that the docking of loop 258–263 into the secondary calcium-independent carbohydrate-binding cleft, which is not found in other C-type lectins (Chatwell et al., 2008), mediates the assembly of the langerin lattice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis with citation.

claim: The secondary carbohydrate-binding cleft is not found in other C-type lectins.
source: It is noteworthy that the docking of loop 258–263 into the secondary calcium-independent carbohydrate-binding cleft, which is not found in other C-type lectins (Chatwell et al., 2008), mediates the assembly of the langerin lattice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In DC-SIGN, the region corresponding to the secondary carbohydrate-binding site of langerin forms a shallow pocket occupied by two calcium ions.
source: In DC-SIGN, which is another C-type lectin expressed in dendritic cells, and is closely related to langerin, the region corresponding to the secondary carbohydrate-binding site of langerin forms a shallow pocket, that is occupied by two calcium ions (Figure 7A; Guo et al., 2004; Geijtenbeek et al., 2000a; Geijtenbeek et al., 2000b).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The structural difference between langerin and DC-SIGN may account for the inability of DC-SIGN to form Birbeck granules.
source: This structural difference between langerin and DC-SIGN may account for the inability of DC-SIGN to form Birbeck granules despite its high sequence similarity to langerin (Cambi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation.

claim: DC-SIGN cannot form Birbeck granules despite its high sequence similarity to langerin.
source: This structural difference between langerin and DC-SIGN may account for the inability of DC-SIGN to form Birbeck granules despite its high sequence similarity to langerin (Cambi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The secondary carbohydrate-binding site of langerin has weak affinity for mannose and maltose.
source: Another characteristic of the secondary carbohydrate-binding site of langerin is its weak affinity for mannose and maltose (Chatwell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The sugar-binding surface of langerin CRD is less negatively charged than that of DC-SIGN CRD.
source: This may reflect that the sugar-binding surface of langerin CRD is less negatively charged than that of DC-SIGN CRD (Figure 7A; Chatwell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference with citation and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The interaction between the secondary binding site and mannose/maltose is mainly mediated by backbone amide and carbonyl groups.
source: Moreover, the interaction between the secondary binding site and mannose/maltose is mainly mediated by backbone amide and carbonyl groups (Chatwell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The side chains of Glu261 and Asp263 of loop 258-263 may provide the negative charge required for stabilizing oligo-mannose bound to the secondary binding site.
source: It is possible that the side chains of Glu261 and Asp263 of loop 258–263 docked into the cleft of an adjacent langerin CRD provide the negative charge required for stabilizing oligo-mannose bound to the secondary binding site (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural analysis.

claim: The Asp263Lys mutation caused a significant defect in Birbeck granule formation.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, in the present study the Asp263Lys mutation caused a significant defect in Birbeck granule formation.
evidence: This is a finding from mutational analysis.

claim: The secondary carbohydrate-binding site may only be fully functional when two langerin trimers are bound to each other.
source: The secondary carbohydrate-binding site may only be fully functional when two langerin trimers are bound to each other (Figures 6 and 7B).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural analysis.

claim: The effect of the Met260Ala mutation on Birbeck granule formation was unexpected.
source: The effect of the Met260Ala mutation on Birbeck granule formation was unexpected, because the mutation was supposed to be silent in terms of side chain charge.
evidence: This is an observation from mutational analysis with interpretation.

claim: The side chain of Met260 acts as a hook to stabilize the interface between the two intersecting loops.
source: The observed structural variation of the langerin trimer complex suggests that the side chain of Met260 acts as a hook to stabilize the interface between the two intersecting loops.
evidence: This is an inference from structural analysis.

claim: Oligosaccharide ligands are captured by the lateral surface of langerin according to the proposed model.
source: Our model of Birbeck granule formation suggests that oligosaccharide ligands are captured by the lateral surface of langerin (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on structural analysis.

claim: DC-SIGN binds to dengue virus on its upper surface.
source: In contrast, DC-SIGN binds to dengue virus on its upper surface (Pokidysheva et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The difference in ligand-binding manner between langerin and DC-SIGN may contribute to their different carbohydrate recognition preferences.
source: The difference in the ligand-binding manner between langerin and DC-SIGN may contribute to their different carbohydrate recognition preferences (Valverde et al., 2020; Takahara et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations.

claim: Human langerin is a 328-amino acids protein.
source: Human langerin is a 328-amino acids protein composed of an N-terminal cytoplasmic tail, a transmembrane domain (TM), a coiled-coil neck, and a C-terminal carbohydrate-recognition domain (CRD).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A.

claim: A SNAP-tag was fused at the N-terminus of langerin for the purification experiments.
source: We fused a SNAP-tag at the N-terminus of langerin and inserted an HRV3C protease cleavage site between the tag and the langerin sequences.
evidence: This describes the experimental construct design.

claim: An HRV3C protease cleavage site was inserted between the SNAP-tag and the langerin sequences.
source: We fused a SNAP-tag at the N-terminus of langerin and inserted an HRV3C protease cleavage site between the tag and the langerin sequences.
evidence: This describes the experimental construct design.

claim: The SNAP-tag was biotinylated for streptavidin-mediated precipitation of Birbeck granules.
source: For streptavidin-mediated precipitation of Birbeck granules, the SNAP-tag was biotinylated (star).
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: Langerin trimers bind to each other face-to-face via the CRDs, bringing the two layers of the plasma membrane closer together.
source: Langerin trimers bind to each other face-to-face via the CRDs, bringing the two layers of the plasma membrane closer together.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B and represents a model.

claim: Birbeck granules formed in 293T cells overexpressing langerin are a few micrometers long.
source: Addition of yeast mannan induced the formation of Birbeck granules a few micrometers long.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C.

claim: Purified langerin was released from streptavidin-agarose by HRV3C digestion.
source: Purified langerin (arrowhead) was released from streptavidin-agarose by HRV3C digestion.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1D.

claim: Gold nanoparticles were used as fiducial markers in cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Black dots were gold nanoparticles used as fiducial markers.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1F.

claim: 2D classification of Birbeck granules did not converge well due to the continuity of the structure.
source: Although 2D classification did not converge well due to the continuity of the structure, some classes showed a porous structure with a honeycomb-like lattice.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1G.

claim: Some 2D classes showed a porous structure with a honeycomb-like lattice.
source: Although 2D classification did not converge well due to the continuity of the structure, some classes showed a porous structure with a honeycomb-like lattice.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1G.

claim: The transformation efficiency of langerin-expressing 293T cells was approximately 40%.
source: The transformation efficiency was approximately 40%.
evidence: This is stated in the figure supplement legend for Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The central langerin trimer binds to three inverted langerin trimers.
